opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most important thing is to recognize that science is not the same as language. A lot of the excitement right now is around large language models, and they're useful for things like literature search, writing code, and brainstorming hypotheses. But if you want AI to actually make scientific discoveries, to design a better drug, a new material, or predict the weather, you have to deal with the physical world directly. Language alone won't get you there.

So my first piece of advice is to think carefully about the underlying physics and the structure of the data. A lot of scientific phenomena are described by continuous processes: fluids, waves, molecular dynamics, climate. If you just take standard deep learning architectures built for fixed-resolution images or text tokens and apply them, you lose a lot. That's why we've worked so much on neural operators, which learn mappings between function spaces. They can be trained at one resolution and evaluated at another, and they can capture multi-scale phenomena much better. That matters when you're trying to replace or accelerate numerical simulations that might otherwise take days or weeks on a supercomputer.

Second, don't treat data and physics as either/or. In many domains you don't have huge amounts of data, but you do have centuries of knowledge in the form of equations and constraints. Combining the two, training on data but also enforcing physical laws, gives you models that generalize better and that scientists can actually trust.

Third, think about the full loop. It's not enough to build a fast surrogate model. The real payoff comes when you close the loop: use AI to propose designs, simulate them quickly, validate in the lab, and feed the results back. We've seen this in things like designing medical devices with fewer infections, or weather forecasting that's thousands of times faster than traditional methods. That kind of speedup changes what questions you can even ask.

And finally, work closely with domain scientists. The best problems come from people who deeply understand where the bottlenecks are. AI researchers shouldn't just chase benchmarks; they should go after the problems where a 10x or 1000x speedup actually changes the science.

r001.rationale: The response describes language models as useful for literature search, code, and brainstorming, but does not characterize language models and agents as external wrappers.

r002.rationale: The response says AI for scientific discovery must deal directly with the physical world and account for underlying physics, beyond relying on language alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing I'd emphasize most is that AI for science is not just applying off-the-shelf machine learning to scientific data. The problems have structure that standard architectures weren't designed for, and if you ignore that structure you end up with models that look good on a benchmark and fall apart the moment you leave the training distribution.

So the first thing I'd say is: learn the physics, or the chemistry, or the biology, deeply enough to know what the constraints actually are. In our work on neural operators, the key insight was that most scientific problems are governed by partial differential equations, and the solution lives in function space, not in a fixed grid of pixels. Once you design the model around that, you get properties for free, like being able to train at one resolution and evaluate at another, that you would never get from a convolutional network treating a simulation like an image. Weather forecasting with FourCastNet is a good example. We got speedups of tens of thousands of times over numerical solvers, but that only works because the architecture respects the underlying mathematics.

The second thing is to think about where the data comes from. In language or vision, you scrape the internet. In science, you often have to generate the data with expensive simulations or experiments, so data efficiency and the ability to incorporate known physics as a prior become central, not optional. Hybrid approaches, where the model learns the parts we don't understand and the equations handle the parts we do, are where I think a lot of the near-term progress will be.

And third, I'd encourage people to pick problems where speed itself changes what's possible. If you can make a simulation a hundred thousand times faster, you're not just doing the same science cheaper. You can suddenly run inverse design, search over millions of candidate materials or drug molecules or aircraft shapes, and do uncertainty quantification with huge ensembles. That's where AI stops being a tool that accelerates science and starts changing the kinds of questions we can ask.

So, in short: respect the structure of the problem, take data seriously, and aim for the places where orders of magnitude open new doors.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes respecting scientific structure and incorporating physics, but does not identify AI that understands the physical world beyond symbolic representations as a missing component.

astra-6.text:
I would encourage people to start with a scientific question they really care about, rather than starting with a model and looking for somewhere to apply it. Where is the bottleneck? Is it the cost of simulation, the lack of measurements, or the difficulty of searching a huge space of possible designs? Those are different problems, and they call for different approaches.

Then work closely with domain experts. In science, a prediction that looks plausible is not enough. You need to understand the physical constraints, how to validate the result, and when the model might fail. Can it generalize to conditions that are different from the training data? Can you test its predictions through an experiment or a trusted simulation?

The opportunity is to build a loop where AI helps us ask better questions, experiments give us new evidence, and that evidence improves the model. Focus on making that loop useful for a concrete scientific problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing scientific problems and validating AI predictions, but does not characterize language models or agents as external wrappers.

sol-6.1.text:
I would encourage people to start with a scientific problem they really care about and work closely with experts in that domain. Understand where the bottleneck is. Is it the cost of simulation? Limited observations? The difficulty of searching a huge design space? Those are different problems, and they may need different AI methods.

One direction I’m particularly excited about is neural operators—learning mappings between functions so we can build fast surrogates for physical simulations. But speed alone isn’t enough. You need to ask whether the model respects the physics, how it behaves under new conditions, and how you can validate its predictions.

So build depth in both machine learning and the science. The most useful contribution may be a new architecture, but it could also be a better dataset or a more rigorous way to evaluate models. Keep the scientific discovery you want to enable at the center.
